strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: the trade-off between model helpfulness and safety (alignment tax), exploring conditional safety adaptation.

The probing analysis is intuitive, providing empirical observations that representations at the last token from middle-to-late layers of Mistral-7B contain sufficient information to detect malicious prompts.
The manuscript is clearly structured and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The submission is substantially incomplete in terms of depth and length, consisting of only roughly 4.5 pages of core content and lacking the rigor expected for a conference track paper.

The experimental scope is severely limited: experiments are performed on only a single model (Mistral-7B) and evaluated on a single safety benchmark (WildJailbreak). Demonstrating findings across multiple modern LLM families (e.g., Llama 3, Gemma, Qwen) and diverse safety/jailbreak suites (e.g., HarmBench, JailbreakBench, BeaverTails) is essential.

Benign evaluation is inadequate: the authors only evaluate false positives on MMLU-Redux, which comprises standard multiple-choice academic questions that rarely trigger false safety guardrails. A realistic evaluation must include borderline benign datasets prone to over-refusal (e.g., XSTest, WildGuard/WildJailbreak benign contrast sets).

Lack of end-to-end pipeline evaluation: despite proposing a conditional adaptation framework where a classifier dynamically gates a safety LoRA adapter, the paper never reports full system performance (overall safety score, helpfulness, and overhead/latency) operating in this combined setup.

Limited novelty and weak positioning against existing literature: both input-level safety classification/guardrailing and linear probing/representation engineering for safety concepts (e.g., Zou et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Arditi et al., 2024) are well established, and the paper does not offer significant new algorithmic or conceptual insights.

strengths: The core motivation—avoiding capability degradation on benign requests while maintaining safety through conditional routing—addresses an important, practical challenge in LLM deployment.

The analysis of internal representations provides a clear, practical finding: a simple MLP probe on the final token hidden state performs competitively with heavier transformer modules and explicit safety prompting.
The manuscript is written clearly, and the concepts are easy to follow.
weaknesses: The experimental scope is very narrow: experiments are conducted solely on a single model (Mistral-7B) and evaluated on only two datasets (WildJailbreak and MMLU-Redux). Standard safety, jailbreak, and over-refusal benchmarks (e.g., HarmBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, BeaverTails) are missing.

Using MMLU-Redux as the sole proxy for benign utility is insufficient. Multiple-choice domain knowledge questions do not adequately measure conversational helpfulness, open-ended instruction following, or exaggerated safety (false refusals on benign sensitive prompts, which benchmarks like XSTest target).

The novelty of the contributions is limited. Routing unsafe prompts via an input guardrail classifier or representation-based probe is a standard design pattern, and existing literature (e.g., representation engineering and mechanistic interpretability of refusal directions) has extensively documented that safety-relevant information emerges in intermediate and late model layers.

The proposed end-to-end conditional pipeline is not comprehensively evaluated on full conversational generation quality (e.g., using AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, or human evaluation) to demonstrate whether the combined system truly preserves generation quality while preventing harms under diverse attack vectors.

The submission is underdeveloped in length and empirical detail (only ~4.5 pages of core content), lacking essential training specifics such as hyperparameter choices, data splits, and statistical significance across multiple seeds.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and timely challenge in LLM deployment: mitigating the trade-off between safety alignment and general model helpfulness/performance.
The manuscript is written clearly and presents an intuitive, modular framework based on conditional adapter application via internal representation classification.

The comparative analysis between simple token-level linear/MLP probes and full-sequence transformer classifiers provides a clear and practical takeaway regarding the sufficiency of the final token representation.
weaknesses: The manuscript is substantially underdeveloped in scope and depth, spanning fewer than 5 pages of main content and reading more like an initial workshop abstract than a complete conference contribution.

Limited novelty: Using internal representations (probes) to detect safety or harmfulness, as well as conditional routing/guardrailing to specialized adapters or safety models, are established concepts in activation engineering (e.g., representation engineering) and LLM system design.

Evaluation is narrow and insufficient: experiments are restricted to a single model architecture (Mistral-7B) and a single safety benchmark (WildJailbreak). Evaluating across multiple diverse model families (e.g., Llama-3, Gemma, Qwen) and comprehensive safety suites (e.g., HarmBench, BeaverTails, AdvGLUE) is necessary.

Inadequate evaluation of false-positive / over-refusal rates: MMLU-Redux consists of standard multiple-choice academic knowledge questions, which rarely trigger safety filters. Evaluating false positive behavior requires dedicated over-refusal benchmarks containing benign yet sensitive keywords (such as XSTest or OKTest).

Missing end-to-end pipeline evaluation: The paper advocates for a two-step conditional routing system, but does not thoroughly benchmark the complete integrated pipeline (detector + conditional LoRA activation) on combined safety, utility, and latency metrics compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

strengths: Compelling and practical motivation: dedicating a separate large guard model or fine-tuning LLMs specifically for moderation is resource-intensive, whereas extracting safety signals directly from internal representations introduces minimal computational and memory overhead.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 8 harmfulness benchmarks (including adversarial and jailbreak sets like WildJailbreak and XSTest) and 7 neutral capability benchmarks, demonstrating competitive or superior performance compared to specialized guardrails like WildGuard and LlamaGuard3.

Thorough ablation studies examining distance metrics (Mahalanobis vs. Euclidean), model scaling (1B to 70B, dense vs. MoE), layer-wise representation dynamics, sample efficiency, and hierarchical prototype extension for handling new risk categories.
The manuscript is clearly written and well-structured, with intuitive visualizations that effectively support the main empirical insights.
weaknesses: The terminology 'training-free' is somewhat imprecise: while the base LLM parameters remain frozen without gradient descent, the method still fits a Gaussian Discriminant Analysis (GDA) model (computing class centroids and inverting a regularized covariance matrix) over a sizable labeled training set (e.g., WildGuardMix).

The paper lacks comparison to standard representation-based baselines, such as linear probing (logistic regression or linear SVM) or simple activation-addition/steering techniques on the same representations. Since GDA with a shared covariance matrix corresponds to a linear classifier, comparing against a discriminative linear probe would clarify whether the generative Mahalanobis framework confers specific advantages (e.g., out-of-distribution robustness or few-shot sample efficiency).

Evaluation is restricted entirely to input moderation. In real-world deployment, unsafe generations can be elicited by benign or ambiguous inputs that evade input guards, making output moderation an equally critical component of guard systems.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated concept: Instead of training separate multi-billion-parameter guard models or relying on brittle prompting, the authors leverage the intrinsic safety representations already learned by instruction-tuned LLMs via a lightweight, training-free Mahalanobis prototype classifier.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The proposed method is evaluated across 8 harmfulness benchmarks and 7 neutral/benign datasets, spanning multiple base model families (Llama 3, Mistral, OLMo2, OLMoE) and parameter scales (1B to 70B).

Thorough ablation and analytical studies: The paper systematically examines key design dimensions, including Euclidean vs. Mahalanobis distance, shared vs. class-specific covariance estimation, layer depth sensitivity, sample efficiency, and pretrained vs. instruction-tuned representations.

Effective extensibility: The hierarchical prototype formulation provides a neat, parameter-free mechanism to incorporate new risk categories or domain-specific safety distributions without model fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Missing comparisons against standard activation-based baselines: While the paper compares against dedicated guard models and prompting, it does not compare against simple linear probes, logistic regression, or SVMs trained on the same extracted hidden states, leaving it unclear how much advantage Mahalanobis prototype classification offers over a standard linear read-out.

Lack of evaluation against adaptive adversarial jailbreaks: Moderation systems are often targeted by adversarial attacks (such as suffix-based optimization or token obfuscation). The manuscript does not evaluate whether adversarial perturbations that bypass safety filters also fool the latent prototype distance metric.

Sensitivity to thresholding and class imbalance: The method assumes a uniform prior in the Gaussian Discriminant Analysis formulation, but real-world deployment faces severe class imbalance. The paper focuses primarily on F1 and true negative rates without reporting threshold-independent metrics like AUROC/AUPRC or exploring decision threshold calibration.

strengths: Practical and computationally lightweight approach: Latent Prototype Moderator (LPM) enables prompt moderation without training dedicated guard models or fine-tuning, operating directly on the last-token hidden states computed during the forward pass.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is benchmarked against established dedicated guard models (Aegis-Guard, LlamaGuard 1/2/3, and WildGuard) across 8 safety/harmfulness datasets and 7 general capability benchmarks (to ensure a high true negative rate).

Extensive analysis and ablations: The authors provide thorough investigations covering model scales (from 1B up to 70B and MoE), layer depth, sample efficiency with respect to calibration data size, comparison between pretrained and instruction-tuned base models, and hierarchical prototypes for expanding to new threat distributions.

Clear writing and intuitive motivation: The paper clearly illustrates the discrepancy between an LLM's latent safety representations and its generative behavior, providing clean visualizations and solid motivation for distance-based safety classification.
weaknesses: Missing comparison to standard linear probing: Gaussian Discriminant Analysis (GDA) with a shared covariance matrix is functionally a linear classifier in the latent space. The paper lacks comparison to standard linear probes (e.g., logistic regression or linear SVM) fitted on the same hidden activations to verify whether prototype-based Mahalanobis distance offers measurable advantages over standard convex linear classification.

Restricted to input moderation: Unlike dedicated guard models (such as LlamaGuard and WildGuard) which moderate both incoming user prompts and outgoing generated responses, LPM operates solely on input prompts. This operational discrepancy should be contextualized more prominently when comparing against dual-purpose guard models.

Semantic ambiguity of 'training-free': While LLM parameters are not modified, computing the empirical class covariance and inverting the high-dimensional precision matrix requires an annotated calibration set (e.g., WildGuardMix). Positioning this as strictly 'training-free' rather than 'non-parametric / linear post-hoc calibration' can be somewhat misleading.

Absence of adaptive attack evaluations: The paper evaluates on existing adversarial benchmark sets (e.g., WildJailbreak, HarmBench), but does not evaluate robustness against adaptive attacks that specifically optimize prompt suffixes or latent trajectories to evade distance-based boundaries in the activation space.
